subsection: 5. Case study: the Sunningdale Agreement and the power-sharing executive, 1973–1974

notes.h: Background: Stormont, Direct Rule and the parties by 1973
notes.b: Sunningdale only makes sense against the collapse of the old system of government in Northern Ireland. By 1973 Britain was looking for a new settlement that both communities could accept.
points: Stormont was Northern Ireland's devolved parliament (it handled local affairs while Westminster kept overall control), and the Unionist Party had dominated it since 1921. Nationalists felt excluded because of discrimination and gerrymandering (drawing electoral boundaries to favour one side).
Violence escalated from 1969. Internment (imprisonment without trial) began on 9 August 1971, and Bloody Sunday followed on 30 January 1972, so confidence in the old system collapsed.
As a result Stormont was suspended and Direct Rule from London began in March 1972, with William Whitelaw as the first Secretary of State for Northern Ireland.
Direct Rule meant a Secretary of State answerable to Westminster ran Northern Ireland, so the British aim was to replace it with a devolved government acceptable to both communities.

The SDLP (Social Democratic and Labour Party, the main nationalist party, founded in August 1970 by Gerry Fitt, John Hume and others) and the Alliance Party (a cross-community party, also founded in 1970) were the new parties of moderate opinion.
Unionism was split between supporters of reform and power sharing and opponents of both, so any new settlement had to win over a divided majority community.
notes.tip: Date the background accurately: Direct Rule began in March 1972, not 1973. Keep the 1973 border poll, the Assembly election and the 1974 Westminster election distinct.

notes.b: Power sharing was the central idea of the 1973 settlement. It was an answer to the old Stormont system, in which one community held all the power.
points: Power sharing means unionists and nationalists both holding executive office (seats in the government), so that neither community can rule alone.

The executive was the government of Northern Ireland, the Assembly was its parliament, and the Council of Ireland was a separate all-Ireland body. Keep the three distinct, because answers often confuse them.
Supporters argued that nationalists would only accept the state if they shared in running it. Opponents argued that it put into government people who wanted to end the Union.
notes.tip: Define power sharing in one clear sentence at the start of an essay, then use the terms executive, Assembly and Council of Ireland correctly.

notes.h: Background: the border poll of March 1973
notes.b: The first step in the 1973 plan was a vote on Northern Ireland's constitutional position. It was meant to reassure unionists, but it settled less than it appeared to.
points: The border poll was held on 8 March 1973. It asked voters whether Northern Ireland should remain part of the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland.
Nationalists boycotted it, so the result was never going to measure their view.
About 98.9 per cent of the votes cast were to stay in the United Kingdom, but turnout was only about 59 per cent because of the boycott.
The poll therefore confirmed that a majority of those who voted wanted the Union, but it did not settle the question for nationalists, since the boycott left their view unrecorded.
notes.tip: The border poll (March 1973) is a different event from the Assembly election (June 1973). Give the date, the boycott, the result and the turnout.

notes.h: The 1973 White Paper and the Constitution Act
notes.b: With the poll held, Britain set out its plan for a new devolved government. It combined power sharing inside Northern Ireland with a link to the Republic.
points: The White Paper (a government policy document) of March 1973, Northern Ireland Constitutional Proposals, proposed an Assembly elected by proportional representation, so that minority parties would win seats in line with their votes.
It also proposed an executive in which unionists and nationalists shared power, meaning that power sharing would be built into the government itself.

The White Paper proposed a Council of Ireland linking Belfast and Dublin as an Irish dimension (a recognised role for the Republic). Many unionists regarded this as a first step towards a united Ireland.
The Northern Ireland Constitution Act of July 1973 abolished the old Stormont parliament, so that the new Assembly could replace it.
Under the Act the Secretary of State kept responsibility for security, so the new executive would not control the police or army.
notes.tip: This Council of Ireland is the 1973 proposal. Do not confuse it with the earlier Council of Ireland in the Government of Ireland Act of 1920.

notes.b: The Assembly election tested whether power sharing had enough support. It showed how badly unionism had split.
points: The Assembly election was held on 28 June 1973 and used the single transferable vote (a form of proportional representation in which voters rank candidates and surplus votes transfer), which gave small parties a fair chance of seats.
The Assembly had 78 members. The SDLP won 19 seats and the Alliance Party won 8.
Unionists were divided between Faulkner's supporters in the Ulster Unionist Party, who accepted power sharing, and unionists who opposed it.

The opponents of power sharing included unionists inside the Ulster Unionist Party itself, Ian Paisley's Democratic Unionists and William Craig's Vanguard. Unionist seat totals are disputed, so none are given here.
This split mattered because the new system depended on unionist consent, and the party that was meant to deliver it was fighting itself.
notes.tip: Name the single transferable vote and the June 1973 date. Do not claim the pro and anti groups won equal numbers of seats, because the unionist totals are disputed.

notes.h: Forming the power-sharing executive, November 1973 to January 1974
notes.b: After the election the parties that accepted power sharing negotiated an executive. Its make-up shows how power sharing worked in practice.
points: Agreement to form an executive was reached in November 1973, so it could take office on 1 January 1974.
Brian Faulkner (Unionist) was Chief Executive, and Gerry Fitt (SDLP) was Deputy Chief Executive.
John Hume (SDLP) was Minister of Commerce, and Oliver Napier (Alliance) was in charge of legal affairs.
Austin Currie (SDLP) held Housing, and Paddy Devlin (SDLP) held Health and Social Services.
The voting membership was 11: six pro-agreement Unionists, four SDLP and one Alliance. This put unionists and nationalists in government together for the first time.
Faulkner led this executive, but his own party was split, so the party's ruling body would soon turn against it.
notes.tip: Chief Executive in 1974 is Faulkner's title. As Prime Minister (1971-72) he led the old Stormont government, so do not mix the two. Short answers ask for the dates 1 January to 28 May 1974.

notes.b: The executive was agreed inside Northern Ireland, but the Irish dimension needed the two governments. They met with the Northern Ireland parties at Sunningdale to settle it.
points: The conference was held at Sunningdale Park in Berkshire, England, from 6 to 9 December 1973.
The British Prime Minister Edward Heath and the Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Liam Cosgrave attended, along with the three parties that backed power sharing.
The Northern Ireland parties present were Faulkner's Unionists, the SDLP (Fitt, Hume and others) and the Alliance Party (Napier).
The agreement was announced on 9 December 1973, and the British government said it was committed to implementing it.
Heath was Prime Minister at Sunningdale, while Harold Wilson was Prime Minister during the strike. This is a common confusion in dated answers.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph, give the date and place of the conference, who attended and the terms. Each correct, dated statement earns a mark.

notes.h: The terms of the Sunningdale Agreement
notes.b: The agreement dealt with three linked questions: how Dublin and Belfast would co-operate, what the status of Northern Ireland was, and how law and order would be policed.
points: The agreement set up a Council of Ireland with a council of ministers, seven members from each side, to give the Irish dimension a formal body.
The Council also had a consultative assembly (an advisory body without law-making power) of 60 members, 30 from the Dáil (the Irish parliament) and 30 from the Northern Ireland Assembly.
On status, the Irish government accepted that Northern Ireland's status would not change without the consent of a majority of its people. This is the consent guarantee.
The British government declared that it would support a united Ireland if that majority wished it, so consent worked in both directions.
A Law Enforcement Commission was set up to examine how to deal with fugitive offenders (people who fled across the border) and a possible all-Ireland court.
Both governments also promised policing acceptable to both communities, because nationalists distrusted the police.
notes.tip: Essays reward a list of the terms: the executive, the Council of Ireland, the consent guarantee and policing. Learn the numbers (seven from each side, 60 members) because they show precise knowledge.

notes.h: Why Sunningdale was controversial for unionists: Articles 2 and 3 and the Boland case
notes.b: Unionists did not accept the safeguards as enough. Two issues in particular fed the fear that the Republic had not really given up its claim to the North.
points: Unionists saw the Council of Ireland as an Irish dimension that could grow into a united Ireland by stages.
Articles 2 and 3 of the Irish constitution, which claimed the whole island, were not changed at Sunningdale. Unionists argued that the Republic's claim therefore remained in force.
Kevin Boland, a former Fianna Fáil minister, took a court case in the Republic in early 1974 challenging the declaration on Northern Ireland's status.
The Irish government's defence was that the declaration did not alter the constitutional claim to the North.
Unionists used that defence to say the Republic had not given up its claim, which damaged Faulkner's position because he had presented Sunningdale as safe for the Union.
notes.tip: State who Boland was, what he challenged and why the government's defence harmed Faulkner. Give no judgments or dates beyond early 1974.

notes.h: Faulkner's party and the executive in office, January to May 1974
notes.b: The executive took office with its own party turning against it. Faulkner lost the leadership of his party within days, and the government's practical work was overshadowed by the row over the Council of Ireland.
points: The Ulster Unionist Council (the party's ruling body) voted by 427 to 374 on 4 January 1974 to reject the Council of Ireland.
Faulkner resigned as party leader on 7 January 1974, and Harry West replaced him as leader of the Ulster Unionist Party.
Faulkner later formed the Unionist Party of Northern Ireland in 1974, because he was now Chief Executive without his old party behind him.
The executive's work on housing, health and education was overshadowed by the argument over the Council of Ireland, which Faulkner tried to postpone.
The executive lasted only about five months, from 1 January to 28 May 1974.
notes.tip: The Ulster Unionist Council (UUC) is the party's ruling body. The United Ulster Unionist Council (UUUC) is the anti-Sunningdale alliance. Mixing them up costs marks, so use the dated 427 to 374 vote correctly.

notes.h: Opposition: the UUUC and the Westminster election of February 1974
notes.b: Unionists opposed to Sunningdale organised themselves, and the Westminster election gave them a powerful argument that the people of Northern Ireland did not back the agreement.
points: The United Ulster Unionist Council (UUUC) was formed in January 1974 by unionists opposed to Sunningdale: Paisley's supporters, Vanguard (Craig) and anti-Faulkner Unionists (West).
Paisley's role in the UUUC was as a leader of the opposition to Sunningdale, which is why his supporters were central to it.
In the Westminster general election of 28 February 1974 the UUUC won 11 of the 12 Northern Ireland seats. Gerry Fitt held Belfast West for the SDLP.
No party won a majority in Britain, and Harold Wilson formed a Labour government in March 1974, with Merlyn Rees as Secretary of State. Rees followed William Whitelaw, who held the post in 1972-73.
Unionist opponents argued that the result showed the agreement was imposed on the majority, and they used this claim to justify the strike.
notes.tip: Do not say the Conservatives lost the election outright: no party won a majority, and Wilson formed a Labour government in March 1974. Heath was Prime Minister at Sunningdale, Wilson at the strike.

notes.h: The Ulster Workers' Council strike, May 1974
notes.b: The strike was the event that finally broke the executive. It showed that a determined protest by loyalist workers could stop Northern Ireland running.
points: The Assembly voted by 44 to 28 on 14 May 1974 to support the Sunningdale policy, and the strike began the next day, 15 May 1974.

The Ulster Workers' Council (UWC) led the strike. Its chairman was Harry Murray, and it was supported by loyalist paramilitaries, the UDA and UVF. Glenn Barr and Andy Tyrie were also associated with the strike as other leaders.
The strike drew on workers in power generation and essential industries, and it was enforced by roadblocks and intimidation.
Power output was cut, fuel became short and services were paralysed, which meant the executive could not govern.
The Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 17 May 1974, two days after the strike began, killed 33 people in the Republic.
notes.tip: Do not mix the Ulster Workers' Council (the strike organisers) with the UDA, the loyalist paramilitary group that backed it. A document question on the strike expects you to place it in May 1974 and judge reliability.

notes.h: The British response and the collapse, 25 to 28 May 1974
notes.b: London did not defend the executive. Its failure to confront the strikers, and a broadcast that angered unionists, left Faulkner with nothing to bargain with.
points: Merlyn Rees refused to negotiate with the UWC, and the army did not take on the strikers directly, so the executive could not restore services.

Wilson made a televised broadcast on 25 May 1974 accusing the strikers and their backers of 'sponging' on Westminster and British democracy. It became known as the 'spongers' broadcast and angered unionists.
Faulkner proposed delaying the later stages of the Council of Ireland, hoping to win back unionist support.
The SDLP and Alliance rejected the delay proposal, so Faulkner resigned as Chief Executive on 28 May 1974, which ended the executive.
The executive had lasted from 1 January to 28 May 1974, about five months.
notes.tip: Give the delay proposal, rejected by SDLP and Alliance, as the reason for Faulkner's resignation. For the 'spongers' broadcast give the date, 25 May 1974, and its effect on unionists.

notes.b: The collapse had several causes. In an essay, rank them rather than listing them, with the Council of Ireland, the strike and British weakness at the top.
points: Unionists rejected the Council of Ireland as a step towards a united Ireland, which many believed was the aim of the nationalists in the executive.
The power-sharing arrangements were not supported by a majority of unionists, and the Unionist Party's own members split over the agreement.
The UWC strike showed that a determined protest by loyalist workers could paralyse Northern Ireland's economy and government.
The British government's reluctance to use force against the strikers signalled to unionists that London would not defend the executive.
The Boland case allowed unionists to say the Republic had not given up its claim to the North, so it damaged Faulkner's standing among unionists.
Republican violence continued during the executive's term, and this made moderate unionists more fearful about security and nationalist intentions.
The Labour government of 1974 was weaker in its commitment than Heath's government at Sunningdale, which left the executive with less backing.
The executive had no mechanism to build consent among the unionist community, which was essential to any settlement that depended on majority support.
notes.tip: A strong answer states a thesis and ranks the causes: unionist rejection of the Council of Ireland, the UWC strike and British weakness. Narrative without ranking scores poorly.

notes.h: Key personality: Brian Faulkner (part 2 and overall evaluation)
notes.b: Faulkner accepted power sharing at Sunningdale and paid the political price. His record shows both courage and a misreading of unionist opinion.
points: Faulkner was a Unionist politician, born in 1921. He was Minister of Home Affairs from 1959 to 1963 and Prime Minister of Northern Ireland from 23 March 1971.
He was Chief Executive of the power-sharing executive from January 1974 and was the main unionist negotiator at Sunningdale, taking part directly in the talks with the British and Irish governments.

He defended the agreement to his party but was defeated, since the Ulster Unionist Council rejected the Council of Ireland by 427 to 374 on 4 January 1974. He resigned as party leader on 7 January 1974.
He resigned as Chief Executive on 28 May 1974 after SDLP and Alliance rejected his proposal to delay the Council of Ireland, and he never returned to office.
Contemporaries were divided: loyalist opponents denounced him as a traitor, while nationalists and the British government saw a leader who had taken a risk for peace.
Historians credit him with courage and realism, but argue that he misjudged the depth of unionist opposition and lacked sustained British support.
He later formed the Unionist Party of Northern Ireland, which failed to attract wide support, and his Memoirs of a Statesman were published in 1978.
He died on 3 March 1977 after a fall from his horse while hunting, and he had been made Baron Faulkner of Downpatrick in 1977.
notes.tip: For a Faulkner evaluation, pair strengths (courage, realism) with weaknesses (misjudged unionist opinion, party split) and use the dated points: 4 January, 7 January and 28 May 1974. Contemporary versus later views earns credit.

notes.b: Hume was a key architect of the power-sharing executive, and he argued that cross-community government was the only realistic path to peace.
points: Hume was born in Derry in 1937 and chaired the University for Derry Committee in 1964-65. He was a co-founder of the SDLP in 1970.
He was a leading SDLP negotiator at Sunningdale and served as Minister of Commerce in the executive from January 1974.
He argued for power sharing and an Irish dimension, and believed that a Council of Ireland would give nationalists a stake in the settlement.
He defended the executive in the strike of May 1974, and its collapse confirmed his belief in an agreed, cross-community settlement.
Contemporaries saw him as a capable nationalist negotiator, although republicans, who rejected any settlement within Northern Ireland, attacked him.
Seamus Mallon, his SDLP colleague, later called the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement of 1998 'Sunningdale for slow learners', and historians often link the two settlements.
Hume became SDLP leader in 1979.
notes.tip: For a short Ordinary Level paragraph on Hume, give four or five dated facts: Derry 1937, SDLP 1970, Minister of Commerce in 1974 and SDLP leader from 1979. Link his role at Sunningdale to his ideas.

notes.h: The legacy of Sunningdale up to 1993
notes.b: Sunningdale failed, but its ideas did not disappear. Later attempts to find a settlement kept returning to power sharing, consent and an Irish dimension.
points: The Constitutional Convention, elected on 1 May 1975, tried to restore devolved government but ended in March 1976 without agreement.
After the failure Westminster relied on Direct Rule, with Northern Ireland run from London.
The Anglo-Irish Agreement, signed on 15 November 1985, gave the Irish government a formal role, but it did not restore power sharing.
The Downing Street Declaration of 15 December 1993 was a further attempt to find a settlement.
Seamus Mallon's remark that the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement of 1998 was 'Sunningdale for slow learners' reflects the link historians draw between 1973 and 1998.
Sunningdale became the reference point for later debate on whether any settlement could be imposed without majority unionist consent.
notes.tip: Importance essays compare Sunningdale with the Anglo-Irish Agreement or the Downing Street Declaration. Link its principles, consent and an Irish dimension, to those later documents.

notes.b: Historians judge Sunningdale as both a first and a failure. Weigh the achievements against the limits, and the contemporary views against later ones.
points: Achievement: Sunningdale produced the first power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland, with unionists and nationalists in government together.
Achievement: the agreement set out principles, consent and an Irish dimension, that later settlements built on.
Failure: the executive lasted only about five months, from 1 January to 28 May 1974, and it could not survive a general strike.
Failure: the agreement lacked the consent of the majority of unionists, and the Council of Ireland was rejected as a threat to the Union.
Contemporary view: the British and Irish governments and the SDLP regarded Sunningdale as a sound basis for peace.
Contemporary view: the UUUC and the Ulster Workers' Council regarded it as a betrayal of the Union and a surrender to republicans.
Later view: historians judge Sunningdale a failure, because it showed both that a settlement was possible and that it was difficult when it needed unionist consent.
Later view: the collapse showed that no executive could survive without the support of a majority of unionists, a lesson applied in later talks.
notes.tip: Pair each achievement with a failure, and contemporary views with later ones. Judgement, not narrative, earns the higher marks.

keyTerms.definition: A system of government in which unionists and nationalists share executive power, so that neither community can rule the other.
The body proposed at Sunningdale to link Northern Ireland and the Republic through a council of ministers and a consultative assembly.
The general strike of 15 to 28 May 1974 that paralysed essential services and brought down the power-sharing executive.
The United Ulster Unionist Council, formed in January 1974 to oppose the Sunningdale settlement, which won eleven of twelve Northern Ireland seats at the 1974 Westminster election.
The system of proportional representation used for the 1973 Assembly election, which allowed voters to rank candidates in order of preference.
The referendum of 8 March 1973 on whether Northern Ireland should remain in the United Kingdom, which nationalists boycotted.
The agreement of December 1973 between the British and Irish governments and the pro-Assembly parties, setting out power sharing, a Council of Ireland and a guarantee of consent.
The power-sharing government of January to May 1974, with Brian Faulkner as Chief Executive and Gerry Fitt as Deputy Chief Executive.
A legal challenge by Kevin Boland to the Irish government's declaration on Northern Ireland's status at Sunningdale, which unionists saw as proof the claim remained.

factCards.definition: The conference was held at Sunningdale Park in Berkshire from 6 to 9 December 1973.
Edward Heath, Liam Cosgrave, Brian Faulkner, Gerry Fitt, John Hume and Oliver Napier took part in the talks.
The executive took office on 1 January 1974, with Brian Faulkner as Chief Executive.
The Assembly election was held on 28 June 1973 under the single transferable vote.
About 98.9 per cent of those voting chose to remain in the United Kingdom on 8 March 1973, but turnout was only about 59 per cent as nationalists boycotted it.
The United Ulster Unionist Council was formed in January 1974 by parties opposed to Sunningdale.
